stims.text: S01. Species as distinguishable but changing groups. Learning demand: Explain how species can be recognizable biological groups even though their members vary and species change through evolution. Required facets: (1) Distinguish variation among members of a group from differences between groups, using simple morphological or genetic cluster plots. (2) Explain that recognizable clustering is evidence of biological grouping, while no single plotted trait is a universal species test. (3) Explain why evolving populations and the splitting of lineages make a universally sharp species definition difficult. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S02. Biological species membership. Learning demand: State the biological species criterion and apply it to reproductive evidence. Required facets: (1) Recall that the biological species concept concerns actually or potentially interbreeding populations reproductively isolated from other such populations. (2) Require viable, fertile offspring rather than mating or the production of any offspring alone. (3) Apply the criterion to unfamiliar cases, distinguishing reproductive incompatibility from lack of opportunity to meet; geographic separation alone does not establish distinct species. (4) Recognize when reproductive evidence supplied in a case is insufficient to reach a classification. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S03. Genetic exchange and species cohesion. Learning demand: Explain how genetic exchange connects populations and can oppose their divergence. Required facets: (1) Explain how reproduction and movement among connected populations allow alleles to spread through a shared gene pool. (2) Explain how reproductive barriers restrict exchange between groups and allow their genetic histories to differ. (3) Explain why gene flow can homogenize populations and counter divergence; do not claim that any amount of gene flow makes divergence impossible. (4) Treat a relatively closed species gene pool as a useful model with exceptions, including incomplete isolation and hybridization. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S04. When reproductive evidence is usable. Learning demand: Decide whether the biological species criterion is applicable and whether available reproductive evidence is sufficient. Required facets: (1) Recognize that the interbreeding criterion is inapplicable to strictly asexual reproduction and cannot be tested directly in extinct organisms known only from fossils. (2) Distinguish practical barriers to testing from biological evidence: a failed laboratory mating can reflect unnatural conditions, and observing offspring does not yet establish their fertility. (3) Choose a usable kind of evidence for a stated case, drawing on morphology, DNA, ecology, or ancestry when reproductive evidence is unavailable. (4) Distinguish an inapplicable criterion, an inconclusive test, and positive evidence of reproductive isolation. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S05. Identification by appearance and its exceptions. Learning demand: Use morphological similarity cautiously and distinguish variation within a species from similar-looking different species. Required facets: (1) Recall the morphospecies criterion and the meanings of polymorphism and cryptic species. (2) Recognize that sex, age, or life stage can produce large differences within one species. (3) Recognize that distinct species can look similar and may require genetic or reproductive evidence to distinguish them. (4) Apply the distinction in new cases; visual similarity and visual difference are useful evidence but neither is invariably decisive. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S06. Identification using DNA. Learning demand: Describe and use the chapter's basic DNA-identification procedure. Required facets: (1) Compare an appropriate sequence from a specimen with corresponding reference sequences linked to identified species, as in a DNA barcode database. (2) Use the supplied reference comparisons to identify a specimen or recognize that the evidence does not resolve its identity. (3) Recognize how molecular evidence can reveal distinctions missed by appearance; do not use any DNA difference as an automatic new-species cutoff. (4) Use sequence comparisons supplied in the question; memorizing sequences, using a live database, and inventing a universal percentage threshold are outside this target. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S07. Incomplete species boundaries. Learning demand: Explain how recognizable species can sometimes exchange genes without merging into one undifferentiated population. Required facets: (1) Explain that hybridization and the extent of reproductive isolation can differ among locations or populations. (2) Explain how reduced success of hybrids can help maintain distinct populations despite some genetic exchange. (3) Explain why these cases complicate an absolute interbreeding definition and an entirely closed gene-pool model. (4) Use the distinction between recognizable lineages and complete reproductive isolation without assuming that every species pair hybridizes. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S08. Species identification through ecology. Learning demand: Use ecological requirements as evidence about species boundaries and explain the basis and limits of that criterion. Required facets: (1) Describe a niche through an organism's role, habitat requirements, and resource use at the level introduced in this chapter. (2) Explain how extensive overlap in resource requirements can create competition and how ecological differentiation can distinguish lineages. (3) Apply ecological evidence to asexual lineages and combine it with ancestry evidence when provided. (4) Treat niche differences as evidence to evaluate, rather than claiming that any difference in diet proves separate species or that the chapter establishes a universal numerical niche cutoff. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S09. Species identification through ancestry. Learning demand: Use ancestry evidence while recognizing why common ancestry alone does not determine a species boundary. Required facets: (1) Interpret shared ancestors and nested groups in the simple branching diagrams needed for this chapter. (2) Explain how common ancestry and lineage identity contribute to a phylogenetic species criterion. (3) Apply the criterion cautiously: all descendants of a distant ancestor need not constitute one species, and the relevant scale must be specified. (4) Combine ancestry with ecological or other evidence instead of treating a shared ancestor as sufficient by itself. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S10. Recognizing reproductive barriers. Learning demand: Name a reproductive barrier from a case and classify it as acting before or after fertilization. Required facets: (1) Recall and distinguish prezygotic barriers, which act before fertilization, from postzygotic barriers, which act after fertilization. (2) Recognize and name all six prezygotic types taught here: geographic, ecological, temporal, behavioral, gametic, and mechanical. (3) Recognize and name both postzygotic outcomes: hybrid inviability and hybrid sterility. (4) Classify unfamiliar cases using the actual point of interruption. Correctly classifying one type does not demonstrate knowledge of the remaining types. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S11. Barriers to encountering or accepting a mate. Learning demand: Explain how differences in location, habitat use, timing, or courtship prevent reproduction. Required facets: (1) Trace how geographic separation prevents encounters and how different habitats or host plants can separate mating even within one area. (2) Trace how different breeding seasons or activity periods prevent reproductive encounters. (3) Trace how different courtship signals or responses prevent acceptance of a mate. (4) Explain each of these mechanisms and what a change in the relevant barrier would alter; knowing the category name alone is insufficient. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S12. Mechanical and gametic barriers. Learning demand: Explain how reproduction can fail even when organisms or their gametes encounter one another. Required facets: (1) Explain how incompatible reproductive anatomy can prevent successful mating. (2) Explain how pollen-flower or sperm-egg incompatibility can prevent fertilization, including specific recognition interactions at the cell surface. (3) Distinguish failure of mating from failure of gamete compatibility and trace the interrupted step in each case. (4) Explain the mechanism in a supplied unfamiliar example without requiring organism-specific protein names. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S13. Failure after fertilization. Learning demand: Explain why a hybrid may fail to develop or may develop successfully but remain infertile. Required facets: (1) Distinguish failure of development or survival from failure to produce functional gametes. (2) Explain how incompatible parental genetic contributions can disrupt development. (3) Use prior knowledge of meiosis to explain how chromosome mismatches can interfere with pairing and hybrid fertility. (4) Explain the chapter's general tendency for more genetically similar species to have fewer incompatibilities, without treating relatedness or chromosome count alone as an infallible test. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S14. Reproductive investment and barrier timing. Learning demand: Explain why an earlier reproductive barrier can avoid costs that a later barrier permits. Required facets: (1) Trace time, energy, or resources invested in mating, embryo production, or offspring support when the outcome produces no fertile descendants. (2) Explain how a barrier before fertilization can avoid some of those expenditures. (3) Explain that both prezygotic and postzygotic barriers restrict genetic exchange despite their different points of action. (4) Do not infer that organisms intentionally choose barriers or that postzygotic barriers are ineffective. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S15. From divergence to reproductive isolation. Learning demand: Explain how separated populations can gradually become reproductively incompatible and recognize intermediate states. Required facets: (1) Connect different mutations and their fixation in separated populations to accumulating genetic differences and the eventual emergence of reproductive incompatibilities. (2) Explain why separation alone does not immediately create new species and why reproductive isolation can arise as a by-product of divergence. (3) Recall the meaning of partial reproductive isolation and relate it to reduced hybrid viability or fertility. (4) Recall the meaning of subspecies as differentiated forms within a species, sometimes represented by an additional scientific-name designation; differentiation alone does not establish full reproductive isolation. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S16. Geographic routes to separation. Learning demand: Distinguish allopatric from sympatric histories and distinguish dispersal from vicariance. Required facets: (1) Recall that allopatric divergence involves geographic separation, whereas sympatric divergence occurs in the same geographic area. (2) Recall and apply dispersal as movement that establishes a separate population and vicariance as a new barrier dividing an existing distribution. (3) Classify maps or timelines using locations during divergence, not only where species occur today. (4) Recognize that either route to geographic separation still requires the development of reproductive isolation for speciation. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S17. Divergence in a small peripheral population. Learning demand: Recognize a peripatric situation and explain why divergence may be especially pronounced there. Required facets: (1) Identify a small population established outside the main population's range as the defining setting of the peripatric model. (2) Explain how stronger drift in a small population and different environmental selection can contribute to divergence from the main population. (3) Apply the model to literal islands and isolated habitat patches such as mountaintops or separated forest patches. (4) Interpret greater differentiation of peripheral populations as evidence consistent with the model, while distinguishing differentiated subspecies from demonstrated new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S18. Adaptive radiation. Learning demand: Recognize conditions favorable to rapid ecological diversification and explain their contribution. Required facets: (1) Identify diversification from a common ancestor into multiple species with different ecological roles as adaptive radiation, rather than any increase in population size. (2) Explain how unused resources and release from competitors create ecological opportunity and change selection on traits. (3) Explain how opportunities for population isolation can combine with ecological opportunity to promote diversification. (4) Interpret the chapter's finch patterns of branching, bill-resource associations, and island availability using this mechanism; memorizing finch species names or counts is unnecessary. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S19. Co-speciation. Learning demand: Explain how host speciation can lead to corresponding speciation in associated parasites. Required facets: (1) Trace how a host lineage splitting can separate the parasite populations associated with each descendant host. (2) Explain how the separated parasite populations can diverge genetically and become reproductively isolated. (3) Use this mechanism to interpret corresponding branching patterns in host and parasite trees. (4) Treat matching tree patterns as evidence consistent with co-speciation, not conclusive proof by appearance alone; no detailed later-chapter tree-building method is required. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S20. Divergence despite geographic overlap. Learning demand: Explain the chapter's disruptive-selection route to sympatric speciation. Required facets: (1) Explain the tension between genetic exchange that homogenizes populations and selection favoring different ecological specialists. (2) Trace how an environment favoring extremes but disadvantaging intermediate hybrids can reduce the hybrids' contribution to later generations. (3) Explain how sufficiently strong and sustained selection of this kind can counter homogenization and permit divergence despite geographic overlap. (4) Apply this particular model without claiming that disruptive selection guarantees speciation or that every sympatric route, including chromosome-set changes, requires this same mechanism. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S21. Evidence about a speciation history. Learning demand: Evaluate whether geographic, genetic, and reproductive evidence supports a proposed speciation history. Required facets: (1) Use a vicariance model to predict close relatives on opposite sides of a newly formed barrier, and distinguish genetic relatedness from direct evidence of reproductive isolation. (2) Explain how dated barriers or island formation constrain timing while recognizing uncertainty about dispersal dates. (3) Evaluate sympatric-origin claims against alternative histories involving past isolation and subsequent migration; present overlap alone is insufficient. (4) Apply these evidential distinctions to supplied shrimp, island-palm, or periodically fragmented-lake cases without memorizing their names, dates, or locations. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S22. New species through hybridization. Learning demand: Determine when hybridization has produced a new species and explain how a distinct lineage becomes established. Required facets: (1) Distinguish producing one hybrid from establishing a reproductively persistent lineage distinct from parental lineages. (2) Explain how a viable genetic combination can support fertile descendants while maintaining reproductive differences from parents. (3) Explain how a different ecological role or resource use can help the new lineage persist. (4) Apply the conditions to plant and animal cases; recognize that reproductive isolation can arise rapidly, while neither every hybrid nor every hybrid lineage is a new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S23. New species through chromosome-set changes. Learning demand: Distinguish the origins of auto- and allopolyploids and explain how chromosome-set changes can contribute to speciation. Required facets: (1) Recall and apply autopolyploid to origins within one species and allopolyploid to origins involving different species. (2) Use prior knowledge of chromosome sets and nondisjunction to trace unreduced gametes or genome doubling in a supplied example; hybridization alone does not automatically double a genome. (3) Explain how compatible chromosome sets can permit reproduction within the new lineage while crosses with parental forms may be impaired; a changed chromosome count alone does not prove a new species. (4) Interpret chromosome complements, recognize the chapter's greater emphasis on this route in plants, and explain why excess even chromosome numbers are consistent with repeated genome doubling. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S24. The relationship between selection and speciation. Learning demand: Judge whether natural selection is necessary or sufficient for speciation and explain that judgment. Required facets: (1) Distinguish adaptation within a lineage from the origin of reproductively distinct lineages. (2) Explain how divergence involving drift can contribute to reproductive isolation without selection driving that divergence. (3) Explain how different selection pressures can promote divergence and how selection can also occur without a species splitting. (4) Use these mechanisms to reject both the claim that all speciation requires natural selection and the claim that selection always produces new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

slots.topic: Species and speciation: Chapter 21 of Biology: How Life Works, fourth edition (2023). Undergraduate biology. Species criteria and their limits, reproductive barriers, mechanisms of speciation, and evidence about speciation history. Mutation, selection, drift, meiosis, and chromosome sets are supporting prior knowledge; teach their new connections to speciation within the selected target.

S15. From divergence to reproductive isolation. Learning demand: Explain how separated populations can gradually become reproductively incompatible and recognize intermediate states. Required facets: (1) Connect different mutations and their fixation in separated populations to accumulating genetic differences and the eventual emergence of reproductive incompatibilities. (2) Explain why separation alone does not immediately create new species and why reproductive isolation can arise as a by-product of divergence. (3) Recall the meaning of partial reproductive isolation and relate it to reduced hybrid viability or fertility. (4) Recall the meaning of subspecies as differentiated forms within a species, sometimes represented by an additional scientific-name designation; differentiation alone does not establish full reproductive isolation. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S16. Geographic routes to separation. Learning demand: Distinguish allopatric from sympatric histories and distinguish dispersal from vicariance. Required facets: (1) Recall that allopatric divergence involves geographic separation, whereas sympatric divergence occurs in the same geographic area. (2) Recall and apply dispersal as movement that establishes a separate population and vicariance as a new barrier dividing an existing distribution. (3) Classify maps or timelines using locations during divergence, not only where species occur today. (4) Recognize that either route to geographic separation still requires the development of reproductive isolation for speciation. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S17. Divergence in a small peripheral population. Learning demand: Recognize a peripatric situation and explain why divergence may be especially pronounced there. Required facets: (1) Identify a small population established outside the main population's range as the defining setting of the peripatric model. (2) Explain how stronger drift in a small population and different environmental selection can contribute to divergence from the main population. (3) Apply the model to literal islands and isolated habitat patches such as mountaintops or separated forest patches. (4) Interpret greater differentiation of peripheral populations as evidence consistent with the model, while distinguishing differentiated subspecies from demonstrated new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S18. Adaptive radiation. Learning demand: Recognize conditions favorable to rapid ecological diversification and explain their contribution. Required facets: (1) Identify diversification from a common ancestor into multiple species with different ecological roles as adaptive radiation, rather than any increase in population size. (2) Explain how unused resources and release from competitors create ecological opportunity and change selection on traits. (3) Explain how opportunities for population isolation can combine with ecological opportunity to promote diversification. (4) Interpret the chapter's finch patterns of branching, bill-resource associations, and island availability using this mechanism; memorizing finch species names or counts is unnecessary. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S19. Co-speciation. Learning demand: Explain how host speciation can lead to corresponding speciation in associated parasites. Required facets: (1) Trace how a host lineage splitting can separate the parasite populations associated with each descendant host. (2) Explain how the separated parasite populations can diverge genetically and become reproductively isolated. (3) Use this mechanism to interpret corresponding branching patterns in host and parasite trees. (4) Treat matching tree patterns as evidence consistent with co-speciation, not conclusive proof by appearance alone; no detailed later-chapter tree-building method is required. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S20. Divergence despite geographic overlap. Learning demand: Explain the chapter's disruptive-selection route to sympatric speciation. Required facets: (1) Explain the tension between genetic exchange that homogenizes populations and selection favoring different ecological specialists. (2) Trace how an environment favoring extremes but disadvantaging intermediate hybrids can reduce the hybrids' contribution to later generations. (3) Explain how sufficiently strong and sustained selection of this kind can counter homogenization and permit divergence despite geographic overlap. (4) Apply this particular model without claiming that disruptive selection guarantees speciation or that every sympatric route, including chromosome-set changes, requires this same mechanism. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S21. Evidence about a speciation history. Learning demand: Evaluate whether geographic, genetic, and reproductive evidence supports a proposed speciation history. Required facets: (1) Use a vicariance model to predict close relatives on opposite sides of a newly formed barrier, and distinguish genetic relatedness from direct evidence of reproductive isolation. (2) Explain how dated barriers or island formation constrain timing while recognizing uncertainty about dispersal dates. (3) Evaluate sympatric-origin claims against alternative histories involving past isolation and subsequent migration; present overlap alone is insufficient. (4) Apply these evidential distinctions to supplied shrimp, island-palm, or periodically fragmented-lake cases without memorizing their names, dates, or locations. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S22. New species through hybridization. Learning demand: Determine when hybridization has produced a new species and explain how a distinct lineage becomes established. Required facets: (1) Distinguish producing one hybrid from establishing a reproductively persistent lineage distinct from parental lineages. (2) Explain how a viable genetic combination can support fertile descendants while maintaining reproductive differences from parents. (3) Explain how a different ecological role or resource use can help the new lineage persist. (4) Apply the conditions to plant and animal cases; recognize that reproductive isolation can arise rapidly, while neither every hybrid nor every hybrid lineage is a new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S23. New species through chromosome-set changes. Learning demand: Distinguish the origins of auto- and allopolyploids and explain how chromosome-set changes can contribute to speciation. Required facets: (1) Recall and apply autopolyploid to origins within one species and allopolyploid to origins involving different species. (2) Use prior knowledge of chromosome sets and nondisjunction to trace unreduced gametes or genome doubling in a supplied example; hybridization alone does not automatically double a genome. (3) Explain how compatible chromosome sets can permit reproduction within the new lineage while crosses with parental forms may be impaired; a changed chromosome count alone does not prove a new species. (4) Interpret chromosome complements, recognize the chapter's greater emphasis on this route in plants, and explain why excess even chromosome numbers are consistent with repeated genome doubling. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

S24. The relationship between selection and speciation. Learning demand: Judge whether natural selection is necessary or sufficient for speciation and explain that judgment. Required facets: (1) Distinguish adaptation within a lineage from the origin of reproductively distinct lineages. (2) Explain how divergence involving drift can contribute to reproductive isolation without selection driving that divergence. (3) Explain how different selection pressures can promote divergence and how selection can also occur without a species splitting. (4) Use these mechanisms to reject both the claim that all speciation requires natural selection and the claim that selection always produces new species. Coverage criterion: assess the specified facets cumulatively from learner evidence; a correct name, one example, or one demonstrated facet alone is partial coverage of this target. Questions may address connected subsets across turns; do not force all facets into one question.

misconceptions.text: Individuals within a species must be identical, so variation within a group means it is not one species.
A geographic barrier immediately turns the separated populations into different species, even if they could still interbreed successfully.
Producing any hybrid offspring proves that the parents belong to the same biological species, even when the offspring are sterile.
Organisms that look alike must belong to the same species, and organisms that look different must belong to different species.
Any difference between two DNA sequences proves that the organisms are different species.
Failure to mate in a laboratory proves reproductive isolation, regardless of the testing conditions.
Recognizable species can never exchange genes; any hybridization must immediately erase the distinction between them.
Any difference in food choice is sufficient by itself to establish that two populations are separate species.
All organisms descended from any one common ancestor must be members of a single species.
Hybrid sterility is a prezygotic barrier because sterile offspring cannot fertilize eggs.
A hybrid that survives and grows normally must also be fertile.
Postzygotic barriers do not restrict gene flow because fertilization has already happened.
An existing population isolated by a newly formed barrier is an example of dispersal rather than vicariance.
Two related species living in the same place today must have originated by sympatric speciation.
Any gene flow makes genetic divergence and speciation impossible, no matter what happens to hybrids.
Every hybrid or organism with a new chromosome count is automatically a new species.
An autopolyploid necessarily originates from two species, and an allopolyploid necessarily originates within one species.
Natural selection is required for every speciation event and will always cause speciation whenever it acts.
Adaptive radiation means that one existing species simply grows to a large population size.
Similar host and parasite trees by themselves prove that every branching event was caused by co-speciation.
